entities.name: Confucius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) was a Chinese philosopher, teacher, and political theorist whose ethical system shaped the governance, education, social structure, and family life of East Asia for over 2,500 years — influencing more human beings for a longer period than any other secular thinker in history. Born in the state of Lu (modern Shandong) to a formerly noble family fallen on hard times, he became one of China’s first private teachers, accepting students from all social strata based on merit rather than birth — revolutionary in an aristocratic age. After decades of itinerant teaching and failed attempts to secure high political office, he devoted his final years to editing the Five Classics (the Book of Songs, Book of Documents, Book of Rites, Book of Changes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals), which became the foundation of Chinese education for two millennia. His conversations with disciples were posthumously compiled into the Analects (Lunyu), the single most influential text in East Asian civilization. Confucius taught that social harmony arises from the proper ordering of five cardinal relationships (ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger, friend-friend), cultivated through ren (humaneness/benevolence), li (ritual propriety), yi (righteousness), zhi (wisdom), and xin (trustworthiness). His concept of junzi (the cultivated person) replaced aristocratic birth with moral cultivation as the standard of nobility. Emperor Wu of Han adopted Confucianism as state ideology in 136 BCE, establishing the imperial examination system that selected officials by mastery of Confucian texts — the world’s first meritocratic civil service, lasting until 1905. Confucian ethics spread to Korea, Japan, Vietnam, and Singapore, becoming the moral architecture of East Asian modernity. The Temple of Confucius at Qufu has been in continuous ritual use for over 2,400 years, and the Kong family genealogy is the longest recorded pedigree in human history (83 generations, 3 million documented descendants).
